The project, which also has a 2.4 megawatt-hour battery energy storage system, is expected to serve more than 6,028 residents. It will provide power to 5,929 residential units, 84 commercial connections and 15 dedicated nodes for productive economic activities.
The commissioning, carried out at the weekend, also marked the groundbreaking of four additional interconnected mini-grid projects in Dukku, Bajoga, Kumo and Kaltungo. The four projects have a combined capacity of 16 megawatts.
Beyond supplying electricity to homes and businesses, the project includes productive-use equipment such as electric tricycles, an electric groundnut oil processing plant, a modular electric rice mill and multi-flour electric grinding machines. The equipment is expected to support transportation, agriculture, processing and small-scale enterprises in the community.
The development came shortly after the Federal Government carried out the groundbreaking of 17.7 megawatts of interconnected mini-grid projects in Iwo, Ibadan and Oyo State on Wednesday.
Speaking at the commissioning, Gombe State Governor, Muhammadu Inuwa Yahaya, described the project as an important outcome of the partnership between the state and the federal government through the Rural Electrification Agency (REA).
He said the project was significant for Gombe because it connected electricity directly to the economic strengths of the people, noting that Balanga was an agricultural community.
The governor said reliable electricity, combined with rice milling, groundnut processing, flour production and electric mobility, would do more than light homes, as it would strengthen the entire local economy.
“For us in Gombe State, this project is significant because it connects energy directly to the economic strengths of our people. Balanga is an agricultural community. When reliable electricity is combined with rice milling, groundnut processing, flour production and electric mobility, we are not merely lighting homes; we are strengthening an entire local economy,” the governor said.
He added: “Our partnership with the Rural Electrification Agency demonstrates what can be achieved when federal and state governments align around a common development objective. We deeply appreciate President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, the Honourable Minister of Power, and the leadership of REA for translating policy into infrastructure that our people can see, use, and benefit from. This is Renewed Hope made tangible at the community level.”
Also speaking, the minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, said the projects reflected the practical implementation of President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda, which he said sought to separate citizens’ access to opportunity from their location.
“From Kwara State and the Federal Capital Territory to last Wednesday’s event in Oyo State, and now here in Gombe, renewable power is spreading across Nigeria with unmistakable momentum,” Tegbe said.
“This is the practical expression of President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s Renewed Hope Agenda: taking investment to communities and expanding the foundations of shared prosperity,” he stated.
The minister said the true value of the infrastructure went beyond basic household lighting and was aimed directly at rural economic empowerment.
“The true significance of these investments will be measured in the daily lives they improve: the farmer who can process produce closer to home, the trader who can preserve perishable goods, the artisan who can power equipment, and the young person who can build a livelihood within the community,” Tegbe added.
The managing director and chief executive director fficer of the REA, Abba Aliyu, said the Balanga project showed the agency’s new direction in rural electrification, moving beyond the number of connections and megawatts deployed to the economic outcomes created by electricity.
Aliyu said while the number of people connected and the capacity deployed remained important, the next stage was to ask what happened after electricity arrived in a community.
He said successful electrification should be measured by whether farmers could process more produce, whether young entrepreneurs could establish businesses, whether mobility costs would reduce, and whether women could increase their productivity and income.
He also said the inclusion of 2.4 megawatt-hours of battery storage showed the REA’s growing focus on reliability and quality of power supply.
Aliyu said access without reliability would limit economic impact, explaining that the agency was increasingly combining storage, intelligent monitoring, productive-use equipment and sustainable operating models in its interventions.
He said the REA was building electricity ecosystems rather than simply installing power plants.
The Balanga project comes as the Federal Government scales up distributed renewable energy to improve electricity supply across the country.
Through the Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme and other REA interventions, the government said it was using public resources to attract private capital and develop a commercially sustainable distributed-energy market.
The government said it was pursuing several solutions at the same time, including strengthening the national grid, expanding interconnected and isolated mini-grids, embedded generation, solar home systems and dedicated renewable-energy solutions for universities, agricultural clusters, markets and productive communities.
